## Analyst Reasoning

**STORY:** This host is a heavily-loaded consumer/productivity laptop (Lenovo Vantage, HP printer suite, Adobe CC, Office, OneDrive, Zoom, Canva, Figma) with no confirmed logon hijack and no unquoted-service-path vulnerability — Winlogon's Shell and Userinit values are pristine and every service path containing a space is properly quoted. The two items that actually decide the verdict are: (1) two AI-branded services — "ChatGPT" (CodexSandboxService.OpenAI.Codex) and "Claude" (CoworkVMService) — both installed under the normally-protected WindowsApps MSIX tree but both configured to run as **LocalSystem**, which is a privilege level far beyond what a consumer chat-app sandbox/cowork helper needs; and (2) two scheduled tasks living in vendor-named folders (\GoogleUserPEH\, \Lenovo\) whose **Author** field is the local machine account ("Example_Machine\Example_Operator01") rather than the vendor, while sibling tasks in the same folder correctly show "Lenovo" or invoke genuine Google Chrome binaries. None of this is proof of compromise, but it is exactly the pattern this fleet has flagged twice before and never fully closed out.

**KNOWN-GOOD:** SecurityHealthSystray, RtkAudUService, MDCoreSvc/WinDefend (ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Platform is Defender's normal install path), Adobe ARM/AGSService/AdobeUpdateService (standard Common Files\Adobe layout), OneDrive/OneDriveStandaloneUpdater, Office Click-to-Run family, Lenovo driver-store services (RtkBtManServ, igccservice, ipf_uf.exe, etc.) — all in expected paths with expected service names, waved through. The lookalike that would NOT be waved through: "Logitech Download Assistant" invoking `rundll32.exe ... LogiLDA.dll,LogiFetch` is technically a T1547.001 interpreter-proxy pattern; it is Logitech's well-known legitimate mechanism, but if it ever pointed at a DLL outside System32\DriverStore it would need immediate escalation.

**HYPOTHESES:**
- *ChatGPT/Codex & Claude LocalSystem services* — Benign: modern AI desktop apps ship an MSIX-packaged sandbox/VM helper service that legitimately needs elevated privilege to manage containers. Hostile: a malicious or trojanized package impersonating these brands to gain persistent SYSTEM execution. Settling evidence: `Get-AuthenticodeSignature` on codex-windows-sandbox-service.exe and cowork-svc.exe, confirming they chain to OpenAI/Anthropic-signed certificates, plus install provenance (Microsoft Store vs. sideload).
- *GoogleUserPEH / LenovoNowQuarterlyLaunch author mismatch* — Benign: installer ran under the logged-on user's context so Task Scheduler recorded the local account as author instead of the vendor string (common installer quirk). Hostile: a locally-created task disguised inside a vendor's task folder to blend in. Settling evidence: compare the task's XML `<Actions>` binary hash/signature against the known-good Chrome/Lenovo binary and check Security log 4698 (task creation) for the creating process and timestamp.
- *Canva/Figma Agent in AppData* — Benign: standard per-user Electron-style installers that legitimately live under AppData\Local\Programs. Hostile: a dropper reusing those familiar names. Settling evidence: file hash/signature match against vendor-published releases.

**PLAN:** 1) Cheapest, highest-value check first — signature/publisher verification of the two LocalSystem AI services, since a SYSTEM-level foothold is the worst-case hypothesis and a signature check refutes or confirms it in minutes. 2) Pull Security Event 4697/7045 for when CodexSandboxService.OpenAI.Codex and CoworkVMService were installed and by what parent process. 3) Verify the two mismatched-author scheduled task binaries by hash/signature and check Event 4698 creation context. 4) Containment only if any signature check fails: disable the service/task and isolate. 5) Cleanup: re-baseline AppData autoruns (Canva, Figma) and document the Logitech rundll32 pattern as an accepted exception so future audits don't re-flag it.
